note: Curated GTO spots. requiredEquityPct = bet/(pot+2*bet). villainBluffPct = yourEquityPct (% of range hero beats). GTO optimal bluff frequency equals the caller's required equity.

puzzles.title: Facing a small river bet
puzzles.situation: You have top pair top kicker — AQ on a Q-7-2-9-4 rainbow board. Villain fires a small ½-pot bet. Only two cards on the board can beat you cleanly (sets or two pair). Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 30 to win 90. Need 30/120 = 25%. Range: ~18 value combos (sets, two pair) vs ~12 busted draws. Equity = 12/30 = 40%.

puzzles.explanation: 40% crushes the 25% you need. The small bet is the tell — laying you 3-to-1 only needs you to be right 1-in-4 times. Even a top pair facing this price is a clear call against any realistic bluffing frequency.

gto.keyInsight: A ½-pot bet only needs 25% equity to call profitably. GTO bluffs at exactly 25% here — any read tilting villain above that makes calling even better.

puzzles.title: Facing a river overbet
puzzles.situation: You have top pair with a king kicker — KJ on a J-9-5-2-6 board. Villain shoves 200 into 100 — a massive 2x pot overbet. Overbets polarize ranges hard: villain has the nuts or nothing. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 200 to win 300. Need 200/500 = 40%. Range: ~24 value combos (sets, straights, two pair) vs ~6 bluffs. Equity = 6/30 = 20%.

puzzles.explanation: 20% is half the 40% a 2x overbet demands. Big bets punish weak callers — one pair cannot call a range built mostly of value hands. Overbets are designed to make your medium-strength hands indifferent at best.

gto.keyInsight: A 2× overbet needs 40% equity. GTO-balanced villain would bluff at 40% — but this villain bluffs at only 20%, far below GTO. With 80% value hands and just 20% equity, the call is a disaster. One pair folds to polarized overbets.

puzzles.title: The break-even river call
puzzles.situation: Top pair aces, jack kicker on an A-T-6-6-2 board. Villain fires a pot-sized bet — 80 into 80. At this exact price you're on the mathematical knife-edge. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 80 to win 160. Need 80/240 = 33%. Range: ~14 value combos (trips, better aces) vs ~7 bluffs. Equity = 7/21 = 33%. Exact indifference.

puzzles.explanation: This is the indifference point — calling and folding have identical long-run EV. The tie-breaker: calling prevents villain from bluffing you off strong hands for free. At indifference, calling is slightly better because it keeps villain honest.

gto.keyInsight: A pot-sized bet puts hero at exact indifference (33% vs 33%). GTO mixes call/fold here. In practice, call to prevent free bluffs — folding lets villain print money.

puzzles.title: Drawing to a flush on the turn
puzzles.situation: You have four spades — KsQs against As9s4d2c. Any spade on the river completes your flush (9 outs). Villain has a made hand and probes with a tiny ¼-pot bet. Do you call the 25 to draw?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 25 to win 125. Need 25/150 = 17%. Flush draw: 9 spades × Rule of 2 = 18%, exact = 9/46 = 20%. Plus two overcard outs (K, Q).

puzzles.explanation: 20% beats the 17% you need — call. The tiny bet gives you a great price, and your K and Q are extra outs on top that make this even clearer. A ¼-pot bet is almost impossible to fold a flush draw against.

gto.keyInsight: With 9 flush outs on the turn you have ~20% equity. A ¼-pot bet only needs 17% — you have the right price by 3%. Plus KQ overcards add outs if you miss the flush.

puzzles.title: Top pair facing a ½-pot bet
puzzles.situation: Top pair kings, queen kicker on a K-7-2-9-4 rainbow board. Villain bets half the pot — 50 into 100. The board is dry: no flush draws completed, no straight is possible with two cards. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 50/200 = 25%. Range: ~18 value combos (sets, K9, K7, two pair) vs ~13 bluffs (missed Ax draws, QJ, JT). Equity = 13/31 = 42%.

puzzles.explanation: 42% comfortably clears 25%. A half-pot bet on a dry disconnected board means villain's range is loaded with busted overcards and missed draws. Top pair on a rainbow board is a solid bluff-catcher.

gto.keyInsight: Rainbow disconnected boards leave villain with lots of missed draws. 42% of this range loses to KQ — nearly double the 25% needed. Villain is over-bluffing here.

puzzles.title: Second pair vs a small bet
puzzles.situation: Second pair eights on an A-8-3-K-2 board with two big broadway cards. Villain makes a small 40-into-120 stab. You beat all busted hands and missed draws. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 40/200 = 20%. Range: ~15 value combos (AK, A8, top sets) vs ~6 bluffs (QJ, JT, gutshots). Equity = 6/21 = 29%.

puzzles.explanation: 28% beats the 20% threshold. A ⅓-pot bet is almost free to call with any showdown value. Villain only makes this bet unprofitable if they bluff less than 1-in-4 times — an extremely tight range.

gto.keyInsight: A ⅓-pot bet requires just 20% equity. GTO bluffs at only 20% here, but the actual read shows 29% bluffs — hero has the edge. Small bets are cheap to call.

puzzles.title: Top pair vs pot bet — blockers help
puzzles.situation: Top pair queens, ten kicker on Q-J-6-9-2. Villain fires a pot-sized bet. Your ten blocker reduces the number of KT and JT straight combinations in villain's range. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 80/240 = 33%. Range: ~14 value (QQ, JJ, 99, KT straights minus blocked combos) vs ~8 bluffs. Your Ten blocks some KT. Equity = 8/22 = 36%.

puzzles.explanation: 36% just edges out 33%. Your ten eliminates several KT straight combos from villain's range, nudging you from indifferent to slightly profitable. This is a thin call that teaches the blocker concept.

gto.keyInsight: Holding a Ten removes KT straights from villain's value range. That 3% blocker effect is the difference between indifference (33%) and a profitable call (36%). Blockers matter at the margins.

puzzles.title: Eights full — nearly the nuts
puzzles.situation: You have eights full of jacks — a powerful full house. You flopped a set of eights and the board paired jacks. Villain bets 75 into 100. Only KK (kings full of jacks) or JcJh (quad jacks) can beat you — just 4 combos in the entire deck. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 75/250 = 30%. Only 4 combos beat you: KK = 3 combos (kings full), JcJh = 1 combo (quad jacks). Against a realistic ~22 combo betting range you win ~17. Equity ≈ 78%.

puzzles.explanation: 78% is more than double the 30% required. A full house is a value hand, not a bluff-catcher. Even a 75% pot bet only demands 30% — your full house wins 78% of the time. Call or raise, never fold.

gto.keyInsight: Eights full of jacks is nearly the nuts — only KK (kings full, 3 combos) and JcJh (quad jacks, 1 combo) beat you. At 78% equity vs 30% needed, call is mandatory. Raising extracts more value.

puzzles.title: Jack-high flush vs a 2x overbet
puzzles.situation: You rivered a jack-high flush on Jh-9h-5c-2h-Kd — a strong flush but not the nuts. Villain shoves 120 into 60 — a 2x pot overbet. Their range is polarized: a higher flush (Ah+, Qh+) or total air. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 120/300 = 40%. Value: ~10 higher-flush combos (Qh+, Ah+ combos). Bluffs: ~8 missed straight draws (QT, T7 etc). Equity = 8/18 = 44%.

puzzles.explanation: 44% narrowly clears the 40% required. Overbets are balanced at ~40% bluffs at GTO. A jack-high flush beats all the missed-draw air combos — the call just squeezes into profitable territory.

gto.keyInsight: A 2x overbet is GTO-balanced at 40% bluffs. Your jack-high flush beats all the air (44% of range). The thin edge makes this a call — overbets with this many bluffs can't be folded.

puzzles.title: Overpair on a dry board
puzzles.situation: Pocket queens — an overpair — on a very low, dry 8-5-2-J-3 board. Villain bets half the pot. No flush, no clean straight got there. The board is about as safe as it gets. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 50/200 = 25%. Range: ~12 value (sets, J3, A3) vs ~12 bluffs (AK/AT missed overcards, 64 gutshots). Equity = 12/24 = 50%.

puzzles.explanation: 50% is double the 25% required. Dry low boards leave villain with missed overcards and gutshots. An overpair here is not a bluff-catcher — it's a strong hand. Villain's range is 50% air.

gto.keyInsight: Low dry boards have no flushes and almost no straights. Villain's range inflates with missed overcards and gut-shots — exactly 50% bluffs here vs the 25% you need.

puzzles.title: Middle pair facing a tiny probe
puzzles.situation: Middle pair nines on an A-K-9-4-7 board with two big broadway overcards. Villain makes a small 50-into-150 probe bet on the river. Does your showdown value clear the price? Call or fold?

puzzles.explanation: 27% beats the 20% threshold. A ⅓-pot probe says 'I want information cheaply' — villain bluffs this size liberally. Middle pair is a solid bluff-catcher at this tiny price.

gto.keyInsight: Probe bets are information-gathering — villains bluff them more than other sizes. At 20% required equity, middle pair easily qualifies. GTO needs only 20% bluffs; reality shows 27%.

puzzles.title: Ace-high on a 4-card straight board
puzzles.situation: You have ace-high — no pair, no draw. The river completed K-J-T-9 — four to a straight. Any queen makes a straight. Villain pots it. Can ace-high profitably call here?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 100/300 = 33%. Board is overrun with straights (QJ, QT, Q9, etc.), plus two pairs. Only ~4 pure-air bluffs exist. Equity = 4/32 = 12%.

puzzles.explanation: 12% is far below the 33% required. Four connected high cards destroy unpaired hands. Villain's range is loaded with made straights and two pairs. Fold immediately.

gto.keyInsight: A four-card straight on the board shifts massive equity to made-straight hands. 88% of villain's betting range beats ace-high here. You need 33% equity but only have 12% — clear fold.

puzzles.title: Second pair vs ¾ pot — ace re-pairs
puzzles.situation: Second pair nines but the ace paired on the river — now there are trips combos everywhere. Villain bets 75% pot — 90 into 120. The re-pairing card always strengthens the bettor's range. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 90/300 = 30%. Range: ~18 value combos (trip aces, AK, A9, KK, 99) vs ~4 bluffs (QJ, JT missed draws). Equity = 4/22 = 18%.

gto.keyInsight: When the ace pairs, villain's trips combos multiply. Now 82% of villain's range beats second pair. You need 30% equity but only have 18%. River re-paierers always hurt second pair.

puzzles.title: Bricked broadway draw — king-high folds
puzzles.situation: You held a live broadway OESD on the turn — K-Q-J-T — needing an Ace or Nine to complete. The river bricked with a 2. Villain fires a pot-sized bet. King-high on a connected board has almost no showdown value. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 80/240 = 33%. King-high loses to any pair. Villain has ~28 value combos (straights: QJ, Q9, 87; two pair: JT, J8, T8; sets: JJ, TT, 88) vs ~3 bluffs. Equity = 3/31 = 8%.

puzzles.explanation: 8% is nowhere near 33%. A missed OESD becomes near-worthless air — king-high even loses to many of villain's bluffs. The gap between your equity and the required price is insurmountable.

gto.keyInsight: Missed straight draws that reduce to king-high are nearly pure air. King-high loses to any pair and most bluffs. Only 8% of this range is purer air — you need 33%. Easy fold.

puzzles.title: Bottom pair vs 2x overbet on broadway board
puzzles.situation: Bottom pair fives on an A-Q-7-K-5 board — three of the top five cards showing. Villain shoves a massive 2x pot overbet. Overbets on broadway boards demand extreme equity. Call or fold?

gto.keyInsight: Broadway boards (A, K, Q showing) connect with every premium preflop range. A 2x overbet needs 40% equity — bottom pair has 13%. Even at GTO bluff frequency (40%), bottom pair is nowhere close.

puzzles.title: Top pair, weak kicker on a 4-straight runout

gto.keyInsight: On K-T-9-J-8, almost any two broadway cards make a straight. 79% of the betting range beats top pair here. You need 30% equity but only have 21% — fold even top pair.

puzzles.title: Missed nut flush draw — ace-high
puzzles.situation: You had the nut flush draw with AcQc on a club board, but the river bricked. You're left with ace-queen high, no pair. Villain fires a ½-pot bet. Your ace is a blocker but has no showdown value. Call or fold?

puzzles.title: Third pair on an AKQ board
puzzles.situation: Third pair sevens on an A-K-Q-7-3 board. Three of the five highest cards in the deck are showing. Villain bets 60 into 120 — exactly ½ pot. Even the cheap price can't help here. Call or fold?

puzzles.explanation: 15% is well below 25%. An AKQ flop hits every premium preflop hand. Third pair beats almost nothing of note. Even the cheap price requires you to be right 1-in-4 times — third pair here achieves 1-in-7.

puzzles.title: Overpair on a four-flush board (close fold)
puzzles.situation: Pocket queens on a 5h-8h-Kh-2h-Ad board — four hearts landed and you hold no heart. Villain pots it. Any heart in villain's hand is a flush that beats you. This is a close spot that tests board-texture awareness. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 100/300 = 33%. Villain has ~18 flush combos (any heart pair) plus ~6 A2/A5/A8 two pair. Bluffs: ~9 combos (JT, 97 missed straights, pocketpairs with no heart). Equity = 9/33 = 27%.

puzzles.explanation: 27% just misses the 33% required. A four-flush board fundamentally changes hand values — overpairs become bluff-catchers, and poor ones at that. Any heart defeats queens completely. This is the close fold that separates level-2 from level-3 thinking.

gto.keyInsight: Four hearts flip the equity of any non-flush hand. Queens go from strong hand to a thin bluff-catcher — and a losing one (27% vs 33% needed). Board texture recognition is the skill being tested here.

puzzles.title: OESD can't afford ½-pot
puzzles.situation: You hold J-T with a 9 and 8 on the board — an open-ended straight draw needing any 7 or Q to complete. Villain bets half the pot. Eight outs sounds like a lot, but does the price work on the turn?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 40 to win 120. Need 40/160 = 25%. OESD equity: 8 outs × Rule of 2 = 16%; exact = 8/46 = 17%. No pair or overcards add meaningful equity. Equity = 17%.

puzzles.explanation: 17% misses the 25% required for a ½-pot call. Even a strong draw like an OESD is not automatically profitable — the price determines everything. A ½-pot bet is simply too expensive for 8 outs on the turn.

gto.keyInsight: An OESD has only 17% equity on the turn (8 outs). That clears ¼-pot (17% needed) but not ½-pot (25% needed). Know your draw's exact equity before calling — draws are not free money.

puzzles.title: Nut flush draw on the turn
puzzles.situation: You hold Ah-Qh on a K-8-4-2 board — the nut flush draw. Nine hearts remain in the deck to complete the best possible flush. Plus your ace is an overcard that pairs for top pair. Villain bets 35 into 80. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 35 to win 115. Need 35/150 = 23%. NFD: 9 flush outs = 20%; plus 3 ace outs (top pair) and 3 queen outs (second pair) = 6 more clean outs. Total ~15 outs adjusted = 31%.

puzzles.explanation: 31% comfortably clears 23%. The nut flush draw alone comes close; adding overcard outs to pair aces or queens pushes equity well above the required threshold. The nut flush draw is one of the strongest semi-bluff hands in poker.

gto.keyInsight: The nut flush draw (9 outs ≈ 20%) plus two overcard pairs adds ~10% equity. At 31% total vs 23% required, this is a clear call — and a great semi-raise candidate since you're a favorite or near-favorite vs bluffs.

puzzles.title: Low flush on a 4-heart board
puzzles.situation: You hit a flush — T-9 of hearts on a board showing four hearts. Your best flush is J-T-9-7-5 (jack-high). But any villain holding the ace, king of hearts, or queen of hearts has you crushed. Villain pots it. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 90/270 = 33%. Value combos: ~14 higher flushes (Ah,Kh,Qh each paired with other hearts). Bluffs: ~4 busted straight draws. Equity = 4/18 = 22%.

puzzles.explanation: 22% falls well short of 33%. A pot-bet on a 4-flush board almost always represents a higher flush or a legitimate bluff using heart blockers. Jack-high flushes are strong in general but become bluff-catchers here — and losing ones.

gto.keyInsight: On a 4-flush board, non-nut flushes are bluff-catchers that are dominated by higher flushes. 78% of the pot-betting range has a better flush. Villain needs only 22% bluffs to break even — not enough for a profitable call.

puzzles.title: Trips on a paired board
puzzles.situation: You have trip kings — your Ks pairs the Kc and Kd on the board. On a K-K-9-7-3 board, only a villain holding 99, 77, or 33 (pocket pairs that make a full house) or a backdoor straight beats you. Villain bets 40 into 100. Call or fold?

gto.keyInsight: Trip kings loses only to a full house (99, 77, 33 — 9 combos combined). With 70% equity vs the 22% required, this call is mandatory. Trips on a board with no straight possible is nearly the nuts.

puzzles.title: Two pair on a paired board

math.reasoning: Pot odds: risk 90 to win 210. Need 90/300 = 30%. Paired board: ~18 value combos (any T makes trips, T9/T6 makes full house) vs ~4 bluffs (Q8, J7, missed gutshots). Equity = 4/22 = 18%.

puzzles.explanation: 18% falls well short of 30%. On a paired board, two pair is critically weakened — the dominant worry is that any villain with a T has trips that crushes your two pair. Large bets on paired boards are heavily weighted toward trips and full houses.

gto.keyInsight: When the board pairs, two pair drops from 'strong' to 'vulnerable.' Any T in villain's hand — and there are two remaining — makes trips. 82% of this betting range beats your two pair. Fold two pair to large bets on paired boards.

puzzles.title: Weak ace on a dry board
puzzles.situation: You have a pair of aces with a weak kicker — A-6 on an A-7-4-2-9 rainbow board. No flush, no straight is possible. Villain makes a small 30-into-100 probe. Your weak ace beats all bluffs and most missed draws. Call or fold?

gto.keyInsight: Weak kicker doesn't kill top pair's value as a bluff-catcher. On a dry disconnected board, only Ax with a better kicker beats you. A probe bet of ⅓-pot only needs 19% equity — 35% makes this a confident call.

puzzles.title: Missed gutshot: third pair can't call

gto.conceptTag: Missed gutshot: just a weak pair
gto.keyInsight: A missed gutshot on a broadway board means your only remaining equity is a low pair. 85% of villain's range beats third pair here. You need 30% equity but have 15% — fold immediately when your draw bricks on a dangerous board.

puzzles.title: Flopped two pair on the turn
puzzles.situation: You have two pair — jacks and eights — on a J-8-5-2 rainbow board. Two pair is a strong hand that beats all one-pair hands and most bluffs. Villain bets half the pot. No flush is possible and the board is disconnected. Call or fold?

gto.keyInsight: Two pair on a disconnected board is a strong value hand — 62% of villain's range loses to it. With 62% equity vs 25% needed, two pair is a call or even a raise to protect against draws and extract value from worse hands.

puzzles.title: Set vs a 2x overbet
puzzles.situation: You have a set of eights — an extremely strong hand on an 8-K-4-2-J board. No flush, no straight is possible. Villain shoves a 2x pot overbet. Overbets polarize villain's range into near-nuts or bluffs — but your set beats almost everything. Call or fold?

puzzles.explanation: 65% comfortably clears the 40% required. A 2x overbet polarizes villain into the nuts-or-nothing — but your set is almost the nuts here. You lose only to KK or JJ, a combined 6 combos. Even at GTO bluff frequency (40%), sets cannot fold to overbets.

gto.keyInsight: Sets are too strong to fold even to 2x overbets. Only higher sets (KK=3 combos, JJ=3 combos) beat you here. With 65% equity vs 40% needed, this is a call — and a raise is worth considering to maximize value from bluffs.

puzzles.title: Two pair dominated on paired board
puzzles.situation: You have two pair — nines and sevens — but the board has a paired nine. On a 9-9-K-7-3 board, any villain holding a 9 in hand makes trips. Villain fires ¾ pot. Your two pair is vulnerable whenever an opponent pairs the paired card. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 70/240 = 29%. Villain has ~20 value combos: any Nx that makes trips-9 (9c, 9h pair with board), K9, 79 (full house), KK, 77, 33 sets. Only ~4 bluff combos. Equity = 4/24 = 17%.

puzzles.explanation: 17% misses the 29% required. On a board with a pair, any villain who holds the paired rank has trips — beating all two pair hands. The K on board means villain also has KK, K9, and K7 in their value range. Two pair folds to big bets when the board already has a pair.

gto.keyInsight: A paired board transfers power to whoever holds the paired rank. Two pair loses to trips, and trips is trivially easy to make here — 83% of villain's value range makes trips or better. Large bets on paired boards signal trips or better.

puzzles.title: TPTK on a draw-heavy turn
puzzles.situation: Top pair queens, king kicker — TPTK — on a Q-J-7-2 board. Villain has many draws available: flush draws (two diamonds), open-ended straight draws (T-9 for a queen-high straight). Even so, TPTK is ahead of most of those draw combos. Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 40/160 = 25%. Range: ~14 value combos (QQ, JJ, 77, QJ, Q7) vs ~9 drawing hands hero beats right now (flush draws, OESD). Equity = 9/23 = 38%.

puzzles.explanation: 38% clears the 25% needed. TPTK is a value hand — you're ahead of all draws right now, and many draws miss the river. Even on a draw-heavy board, top pair top kicker should not be folded facing a ½-pot bet on the turn.

gto.keyInsight: TPTK is ahead of all draws in the current moment. 38% of villain's range are draws that haven't gotten there yet. With 38% equity vs 25% needed, TPTK is a clear call on the turn — even against heavy draw boards.

puzzles.title: Top pair vs check-raise — bluff-catch
puzzles.situation: You have top pair kings, jack kicker on a K-Q-8-5-2 board. Villain check-raised you on the river — a strong signal that is often polarized between the nuts and a bluff. The board is dry with no completed draws. Do you call the check-raise or fold? Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 60/240 = 25%. Check-raise range: ~12 value combos (KK impossible, KQ, K8, QQ, 88, 55, 22) vs ~7 bluff combos (missed straight draws QJ, JT with J blocker plays). Equity = 7/19 = 37%.

puzzles.explanation: 37% exceeds the 25% required. Check-raises on dry boards without completed draws are often polarized bluffs as much as nuts. Your jack kicker is relevant as a blocker to some QJ or JT bluff combos. TPTK is a mandatory bluff-catcher here.

gto.keyInsight: GTO check-raises are polarized: ~37% are bluffs on a dry board like this. Your top pair king needs only 25% equity to call. Since check-raises must include bluffs at GTO frequency, folding top pair gives villain a free bluffing license.

puzzles.title: Gutshot + two overcards on the turn
puzzles.situation: You hold K-T on a Q-J-8-2 board — a gutshot straight draw (need a 9 for 8-9-T-J-Q) plus two live overcards. King is the best card in the deck to hit; T also makes a pair. At a tiny ¼-pot price, is your combo draw worth calling? Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 30/160 = 19%. Outs: 4 nines (gutshot) + 3 kings (top pair) = 7 outs. Adjusted equity: 7 × 2% (Rule of 2) ≈ 14%; exact calculation with implied odds raises to ~22%. Against bluffs hero also has showdown value.

puzzles.explanation: 22% edges out the 19% required. A gutshot plus two overcards is a classic 'combo draw' that turns into equity even without completing the straight. The tiny ¼-pot price makes any multi-out draw profitable — calls with 7 outs are almost always correct at this price.

gto.keyInsight: Gutshot (4 outs) + overcard pair outs (3 outs) = 7 total outs ≈ 14-22% equity. A ¼-pot bet needs only 19% equity. Combo draws (partial draws + overcards) often clear the price threshold that a single-dimension draw cannot.

puzzles.title: Overpair on a connected board — overbet fold
puzzles.situation: Pocket aces — an overpair — on a K-J-9-7-3 board. Villain shoves a pot-sized overbet. This board has many two-pair combos (KJ, K9, K7, J9, J7, 97), sets, and even straights (T-8 makes 7-8-9-T-J; Q-T makes 9-T-J-Q-K). Can aces stand up? Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 120/360 = 33%. Connected board: ~18 value combos (two pairs: KJ/K9/K7/J9, sets: KK/JJ/99/77, straights: T8 for 7-8-9-T-J, QT for 9-T-J-Q-K) vs ~6 bluffs (missed draws, A-high). Equity = 6/24 = 25%.

puzzles.explanation: 25% falls short of the 33% required. Pocket aces are powerful preflop but can become bluff-catchers on connected runouts. K-J-9-7 connects heavily with value betting ranges: sets, two pairs, and two different straights are all possible. This is the key lesson: overpairs must fold to large bets on connected boards.

gto.keyInsight: Pocket aces lose to any two pair, set, or straight here — and this connected board makes those hands frequent. 75% of villain's range beats aces. A pot-bet needs 33% equity; aces have only 25%. Even premium hands fold on the wrong runout.

puzzles.title: Two pair on a straight-heavy turn
puzzles.situation: You have two pair — kings and queens — but the turn is a T, completing K-Q-J-T: four cards to a straight. Any ace makes broadway (A-K-Q-J-T) and any nine makes a nine-high straight. Villain bets ¾ pot. Can two pair hold up here? Call or fold?

math.reasoning: Pot odds: need 60/200 = 30%. Straight-heavy board: any A makes broadway (AK,AQ,AJ,AT = many combos) and any 9 makes 9-T-J-Q-K. Value combos ~20 (straights dominate). Only ~5 bluffs. Equity = 5/25 = 20%.

puzzles.explanation: 20% misses the 30% required. A K-Q-J-T board is one of the most dangerous turn textures in poker. Any ace or nine completes a straight, and those holdings are extremely common in preflop raising ranges. Two pair is a strong hand on most boards but not this one.

gto.keyInsight: K-Q-J-T means any A or 9 makes a straight — and broadway hands dominate preflop ranges. 80% of the value range beats two pair here. Even with two pair, reading board texture is paramount: this turn is a clear fold for all but the very top of your range.
